questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.solution:
$\text{acid} + \text{carbonate} \to \text{salt} + \text{water} + \text{carbon dioxide}$

The effervescence and the limewater test make this the standard identification of a carbonate.

(Acid $+$ metal gives salt $+$ hydrogen; acid $+$ base gives salt $+$ water.)

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Going down Group 1, the elements become:
questions.solution:
**More reactive** going down.

The outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so it is **lost more easily** — and losing it is exactly what these metals' reactions require.

Group 7 shows the **opposite** trend, because those elements need to **gain** an electron.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution because:
questions.solution:
Chlorine is **higher** in Group 7 and therefore more reactive, so it takes the place of bromine:

$\text{Cl}_{2} + 2\text{KBr} \to 2\text{KCl} + \text{Br}_{2}$

The colourless solution turns orange as bromine is released — a clear displacement, and a direct test of the reactivity order.
options: chlorine is more reactive than bromine

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: The noble gases are unreactive because they have:
questions.solution:
A **full outer shell** means there is nothing to gain by reacting — no electrons to lose easily and no space to take any in.

Every other element's chemistry is essentially an attempt to reach the same arrangement.
options: a full outer shell of electrons

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many times more acidic is a solution of pH $2$ than one of pH $5$?
questions.solution: Three pH units, each a factor of ten: $10^{3} = \mathbf{1000}$ times.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a Group 2 element?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{2}$. The group number gives the number of outer electrons for the main groups, which is why a group shares its chemistry.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many elements are in Period 2 of the periodic table?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{8}$ — lithium to neon, filling the second shell, which holds eight electrons.

The length of each period is set by how many electrons the shells being filled can hold.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: How many moles of $\text{HCl}$ are needed to neutralise $1$ mole of $\text{Ca(OH)}_{2}$?
questions.solution:
$\text{Ca(OH)}_{2} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{CaCl}_{2} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

Two hydroxide ions need two hydrogen ions: $\mathbf{2}$ moles.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{1}$ — two sodium atoms release one molecule of hydrogen.

The hydrogen is what skates the sodium about the surface of the water, and with potassium it ignites.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Define an acid and a base, describe three reactions of dilute acids with equations, and explain how a soluble salt is prepared.
questions.solution:
**Acid** — a substance that produces **hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^{+}$)** in aqueous solution, and a proton donor.

**Base** — a substance that neutralises an acid, usually a metal oxide or hydroxide. A base that **dissolves** in water is an **alkali**, producing $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions.

**Three reactions.**

1. **With a metal:** $\text{Zn} + \text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \to \text{ZnSO}_{4} + \text{H}_{2}$

2. **With a base:** $\text{CuO} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{CuCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

3. **With a carbonate:** $\text{CaCO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{CaCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$

**Preparing a soluble salt from an insoluble base.**

1. Warm the acid and add the base (or carbonate) **in excess**, stirring, until no more dissolves.

2. **Filter** to remove the unreacted excess — this is why an excess is used, since it guarantees the acid is all used up and can then be removed.

3. **Evaporate** the filtrate to the point of crystallisation.

4. Leave to **crystallise**, then filter off the crystals and dry them between filter papers.

**If the base is soluble** (an alkali) this method will not work — the excess cannot be filtered off. A **titration** is used instead, to find the exact volume that neutralises, and the experiment is then repeated without the indicator.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Describe how the periodic table is arranged, and explain the trends in Group 1 and Group 7.
questions.solution:
**Arrangement.** Elements are placed in order of increasing **atomic number** (proton number).

• A **group** is a vertical column. Members share the number of **outer electrons**, and therefore their chemistry.

• A **period** is a horizontal row. The period number is the number of occupied **shells**.

**Group 1 — the alkali metals.**

One outer electron, lost readily to form a $1+$ ion. Soft, low density, react with water to give an alkali and hydrogen.

**Going down: more reactive.** The outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, so it is lost more easily. Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and skates about, potassium bursts into a lilac flame.

**Group 7 — the halogens.**

Seven outer electrons, so they gain one to form a $1-$ ion. Diatomic molecules ($\text{Cl}_{2}$, $\text{Br}_{2}$, $\text{I}_{2}$), coloured, and increasingly dense going down — chlorine a green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, iodine a grey solid.

**Going down: less reactive.** A larger atom attracts an incoming electron less strongly.

**The two opposite trends have one explanation:** Group 1 needs to **lose** an electron and Group 7 to **gain** one, so increasing size helps the first and hinders the second.

**Displacement** demonstrates the order directly: chlorine displaces bromine, and bromine displaces iodine, but never the reverse.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Describe how you would carry out a titration to find the concentration of an unknown acid, and calculate the concentration if $25.0$ cm$^{3}$ of the acid needed $20.0$ cm$^{3}$ of $0.1$ mol/dm$^{3}$ NaOH. (The acid is monobasic.)
questions.solution:
**Method.**

1. **Pipette** $25.0$ cm$^{3}$ of the acid into a conical flask — a pipette because it is far more accurate than a measuring cylinder.

2. Add a few drops of **indicator** (phenolphthalein or methyl orange).

3. Fill a **burette** with the standard alkali and record the initial reading.

4. Add the alkali, swirling constantly, until the indicator just changes colour permanently. Record the final reading.

5. **Repeat** until two results agree within $0.1$ cm$^{3}$ (concordant titres), and average those.

**Calculation.**

$n(\text{NaOH}) = c \times V = 0.1 \times \dfrac{20.0}{1000} = 0.002$ mol.

The acid is monobasic, so the ratio is $1:1$ and $n(\text{acid}) = 0.002$ mol.

$c(\text{acid}) = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.002}{0.025} = \mathbf{0.08}$ mol/dm$^{3}$.

**Why the first titre is discarded.** The first run is a rough one, done quickly to find the approximate end point; the accurate runs are then added dropwise near it.

**Why a dibasic acid changes the answer.** Sulphuric acid would need **two** moles of NaOH per mole of acid, so the calculated concentration would be halved. The balanced equation is what supplies the ratio, and no calculation is safe without it.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Compare the properties of transition elements with those of Group 1 metals.
questions.solution:
**Transition elements** (the central block: iron, copper, nickel, chromium, zinc)

• **High** melting points and densities

• **Hard and strong**

• **Variable oxidation states** — iron forms $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$

• **Coloured compounds** — copper(II) blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) orange-brown

• Good **catalysts** — iron in the Haber process, nickel in hydrogenation

• **React slowly**, if at all, with water and oxygen

**Group 1 metals**

• **Low** melting points and densities — sodium and potassium float on water, and caesium melts in the hand

• **Soft** — they can be cut with a knife

• **One** oxidation state only, $+1$

• **White** compounds, giving colourless solutions

• Poor catalysts

• **React vigorously** with water and air, so they are stored under oil

**The contrast in one sentence:** transition metals are what most people picture when they think 'metal' — hard, dense, durable, useful. The alkali metals are metals that behave almost nothing like it.

questions.chapter: Acids, Bases and the Periodic Table
questions.q: Describe the tests for carbonate ions, chloride ions and sulphate ions, and for hydrogen and carbon dioxide gas.
questions.solution:
**Carbonate ion ($\text{CO}_{3}^{2-}$).** Add dilute acid. **Effervescence**, and the gas turns limewater milky.

**Chloride ion ($\text{Cl}^{-}$).** Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate. A **white precipitate** of AgCl.

(Bromide gives cream, iodide gives yellow.)

**Sulphate ion ($\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$).** Acidify with dilute hydrochloric acid, then add barium chloride. A **white precipitate** of $\text{BaSO}_{4}$.

**Why acidify first, in both cases?** Carbonates also give white precipitates with silver and barium ions, and would give a false positive. The acid destroys any carbonate present first — a small step that is worth a mark and is routinely forgotten.

**Hydrogen gas.** A **lighted splint** burns with a squeaky **pop**.

**Carbon dioxide.** Bubble through **limewater**, which turns **milky**.

**Oxygen.** A **glowing** splint **relights**.

**Ammonia.** Damp **red litmus turns blue**, and the gas has a sharp smell.

In an examination, give the **reagent**, the **observation** and the **conclusion** — all three are needed for full marks.
